study.title: 1 Kings 13 The word of God against the false altar and prophetic disobedience
study.overview: The chapter presents two central messages: God publicly denounces the worship invented by Jeroboam at Bethel and at the same time shows that his word also requires strict obedience from his own messengers. The man of God of Judah announces judgment against the altar and gives an immediate sign that the word of the LORD is true. Jeroboam experiences as much judgment as mercy, for his hand dries and is restored. Then the narrative becomes more solemn: the man of God, although he began obeying, is deceived by an old prophet, disobeys the commandment received and dies on the way. The chapter ends with Jeroboam persevering in sin and his house being declared guilty and destined for ruin.

outline.title: The altar of Bethel is condemned and the sign is fulfilled
outline.explanation: A man of God from Judah interrupts the worship of Jeroboam and announces that the altar of Bethel would be judged by God. The prophecy includes a future name, Josiah, which highlights that the Lord governs history. The immediate sign is the breaking of the altar, pouring it from the ash, and the dryness of the king's hand; then the hand is restored when Jeroboam asks prayer, showing that judgment comes with mercy and opportunity of repentance.

outline.title: Refusal of communion with the center of idolatry
outline.explanation: Jeroboam tries to retain the prophet with hospitality and reward, but the man of God refuses because he has received a specific command from the LORD not to eat, drink or return by the same way. The refusal is not personal rudity; it is symbolic separation from the place and system that God had just condemned. His initial obedience shows that the divine word must be followed even in the details.

outline.title: The old prophet deceives the man of God and he dies out of disobedience
outline.explanation: An old Bethel prophet seeks the man of God, convinces him with a false message revealed by an angel and makes him return to eat. Then, while they are at table, the word of the LORD comes to the old prophet to announce judgment to the visitor for having disobeyed. The man of God is killed by a lion on the way, and the strange sign is stopped by the side of the body, without devouring the corpse or the asno - confirms that death was a divine act of judgment, not a common accident.

outline.title: The funeral confirms the word, but Jeroboam remains hardened
outline.explanation: Passers carry the news, the old prophet acknowledges that death occurred according to the word of the LORD and burys the man of God with regret. He asks to be buried with the prophet, expressing that the prophecy against Bethel will certainly be fulfilled. Even so, Jeroboam does not convert; he continues to establish priests of the class of the people and perpetuating his own system. The chapter concludes that this became sin for his house, which would be cut off and uprooted from the earth.

study.context: The text is set in the northern kingdom, under Jeroboam at Bethel, where the king had established an altar and a culture system contrary to the word of the LORD. The chapter reflects a crisis of religious fidelity: instead of hearing the divine warning, Jeroboam supports his own structure of worship. The narrative also shows that there are prophets in Judah and Bethel, but not every religious voice is trustworthy; therefore, the word already given by God remains the final measure.
study.theology: The chapter teaches that God is sovereign over history, capable of announcing an event by name long before it occurs and confirming his word by immediate signs. He also states that worship invented by the human being, albeit politically useful, is abomination before God. Moreover, the text is severe as to obedience: even a true messenger cannot treat God's command as negotiable. The tragedy of the man of God shows that closeness to the mission does not replace fidelity to the mission. At the end, the hardening of Jeroboam reveals that signs, miracles, and warnings do not produce repentance when the heart insists on idolatry. Judgment, therefore, is not arbitrary; it responds to the persistent refusal of the divine word.

scholarViews.insight: The prophecy naming Josiah beforehand highlights the sovereignty and perfect knowledge of God, showing that the word of the Lord is fulfilled in detail.
The message to the king was sent while he was still dedicating the altar, to confront his idolatry before sin hardens the heart even further.
The outpouring of the ash and the rupture of the altar showed that the cult of Bethel became unclean and that the idolatrous system was an affront to the divine majesty.

questions: What does this chapter reveal about the difference between a word actually received from God and a convincing but false religious message?
Why is the disobedience of the man of God treated so seriously, even after he was faithful at the beginning?
In which areas can I be, like Jeroboam, persisting in practices that have already been confronted by the Word of God, without actually converting me?
study.practice: Take complete obedience seriously, not just good intention. Evaluate whether any practice, decision or habit of yours is being sustained by convenience, external pressure or tradition rather than by the Word of God. Also learn to discern religious voices: not all the speech that mentions God comes from God. When the Lord has already spoken, the sure answer is to remain in what he commanded, without negotiating the commandment to fit in personal interests or affections. Finally, do not confuse signs with the approval of sin; the text shows that even wonder before a miracle does not guarantee repentance.
study.uncertainty: The chapter does not identify the man of God by name, nor fully clarifies who the old prophet was or why he lied. The notes also do not allow the degree of subjective guilt of the old prophet in addition to what the text states. The reference to Samaria in 13:32 is understood here only according to the text received, without extending to historical conclusions beyond the notes provided.
